passage: When Hiroshi's name went up on the dean's list at the university in Melbourne, his first thought was: someone made a mistake. He'd got the scholarship because the other applicants had bad days, he told himself; he'd passed Thermodynamics because the exam was easy that year. So he stayed in the library until it closed, every night, rewriting notes he already knew. When his tutor praised his design report, he said, "I just followed the template." One night Lindiwe, from his study group, found him there at eleven. "Can I tell you something embarrassing? I keep waiting for them to take my place back." Hiroshi stared at her. "You too?" They talked until the guard switched off the lights.

qa.q: What did Hiroshi say when his tutor praised his report?
qa.a: "I just followed the template."

qa.q: What was Hiroshi feeling when his name went up on the dean's list?
qa.a: He felt doubtful and afraid, sure it was a mistake and that his success was just luck.

qa.q: What helped Hiroshi feel less alone with the fear?
qa.a: Lindiwe naming the same feeling, which showed him others feel it too.

qa.q: How might Lindiwe feel when Hiroshi says "You too?"
qa.a: Lindiwe probably feels relieved and less embarrassed, finding that someone she respects has the same fear.

grounding: Shows a capable student who calls his success luck, overworks and discounts praise until a peer shares the same fear.

passage: In his third week at the insurance office in Guwahati, Bhupen's manager said in the team meeting, "Bhupen's claims summary is the clearest we've had in months." At the tea counter next morning, Arnab, who'd joined the same month, said, "Nice work yesterday." "Luck," Bhupen said. "Honestly, I feel like a fraud here." Arnab laughed, not unkindly. "I've been looking up basic terms on my phone under the desk for three weeks." Bhupen laughed too, and something in his chest loosened.

qa.q: How late did Bhupen stay that night?
qa.a: Till nine.

qa.q: What was Bhupen feeling when the manager praised him?
qa.a: He felt dread rather than pride, afraid someone would find mistakes and see him as a fraud.

qa.q: Which step helped Bhupen, and why?
qa.a: Admitting the fraud feeling to Arnab, because Arnab's reply showed a new colleague feels the same.

qa.q: What might Arnab be feeling when he admits to looking up terms under the desk?

grounding: Illustrates a new employee who treats praise as luck, over-checks his work and finds relief when a peer shares the feeling.

passage:

passage:

I told her: her calm voice, and that she knows every child's name. She wrote both lists down, side by side, without arguing or over-apologising. On Thursday she retaught the lesson with paper strips. passage: In her first month at the design studio in Manchester, Amara was everyone's favourite: coffee for the team, compliments on every sketch, stories that made the manager laugh. By month four, things were different. She expected the corner desk by the window, and got it. She presented Soo-ah's packaging idea to the client as "something I've been developing". When Soo-ah mentioned her mother was in hospital, Amara said, "Oh no," then asked if Soo-ah could still finish the mock-ups by Friday. Amara was warm when the director was around and bored when she wasn't. She told herself she was simply more ambitious than the others. The team had stopped inviting her to lunch; she hadn't noticed yet.

qa.q: Whose packaging idea did Amara present as her own?
qa.a: Soo-ah's.

qa.q: How does Amara seem to feel about her own behaviour?
qa.a: She seems pleased and self-satisfied, telling herself she is simply more ambitious, with no sign of guilt.

qa.q: What could Amara do if she wanted to repair things with the team?
qa.a: Credit Soo-ah openly, ask how Soo-ah's mother is and stop expecting special treatment.

qa.q: How might Soo-ah feel when Amara asks about the mock-ups right after hearing about the hospital?
qa.a: Soo-ah likely feels hurt and used, as her worry is brushed aside for deadlines.

grounding: Shows a charming newcomer who begins to expect special treatment, takes credit and shows little curiosity about others' feelings.

grounding: Illustrates a charming lead who grows entitled, takes credit and shows empathy only when it serves him.

passage: At the NGO office in Nairobi, Priscila watched it happen again in Monday's meeting. Wanjiru presented the school-meals survey to the director as "my analysis", though Priscila and two interns had coded every form. Later, by the kettle, Wanjiru called one intern's charts "a bit amateur", loud enough for everyone to hear. Priscila felt heat in her chest, and the urge to go straight to the director and outshine Wanjiru. She didn't. That evening she opened a shared document and started listing who did what, with dates and file links. On Wednesday she sent a short, factual email to the team and the director: "Summary of survey contributions attached, for the report credits." She didn't add a single adjective.

qa.q: What did Wanjiru call the intern's charts?
qa.a: "a bit amateur"

qa.q: What was Priscila feeling after the meeting?
qa.a: She felt angry, with heat in her chest, and tempted to compete for the director's admiration.

qa.q: Why was Priscila's email a wise response?
qa.a: It relied on records and facts, protecting the team's credit without a fight for attention.

qa.q: How might the intern feel after hearing the charts called amateur?
qa.a: The intern probably felt embarrassed and discouraged, especially in front of others.

grounding: Shows a colleague who sees credit-taking and belittling, then keeps records and addresses it factually.

grounding: Illustrates a colleague who sees credit-taking and belittling, records contributions and addresses them factually.
